2.1 Out of Africa: The Original Expansion

Approximately seventy thousand years ago, a population of anatomically modern humans, perhaps only a few thousand individuals, began to move out of Africa [Klein 2009]. Africa had been home to humans for hundreds of thousands of years. Within the generations that followed, humans would come to inhabit environments very different from those in which they had evolved.

To do so they had to learn to live in colder climates, cross deserts and mountain ranges, and find food in environments unfamiliar to them. In Eurasia they encountered other hominins. What interests us about this period of human history is why the expansion continued.

There are several explanations for why humans left Africa. Changes in climate may have made it difficult to survive in parts of the continent. As populations grew, there may have been competition for food and other resources. There is also the question of capability. As humans developed better tools and ways of obtaining food, they became capable of living in places where they previously could not.

But much of the human population remained in Africa. We cannot infer from this that those who left did not have to leave. What we can ask is whether the need to survive was the only force at work.

Consider what it means for an animal to be able to imagine an environment other than the one in which it lives, and to plan how it might live there. The capacity to imagine what lies elsewhere may itself give rise to a desire to explore. Planning, on the other hand, gives humans some ability to act on that desire. My hypothesis is that both capacities contributed to human expansion.

The settlement of Australia at least fifty thousand years ago, the movement of people into the Arctic, and the much later voyages of the Polynesians are interesting in this regard. In each case humans came to occupy environments in which they had not previously lived. The circumstances of these expansions were different, and we should not assume that their motivations were the same. But the recurrence of expansion across human history gives us reason to consider whether there is something in our cognitive architecture that predisposes us to it.
